abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Atherosclerosis drives cardiovascular morbidity in diabetes, with endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT) as a key contributor. Whereas epigenetic regulators are increasingly implicated in atherosclerotic progression, the specific role of enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a histone methyltransferase, in EndMT in diabetes-associated atherosclerosis remains unclear. We show that EZH2-mediated H3K27 (histone H3 at lysine-27) trimethylation is elevated in carotid plaques from patients with diabetes and in the aortic endothelium of diabetic Apoe−/− mice. Pharmacologic EZH2 inhibition with GSK-126 attenuated EndMT and reduced atherosclerotic burden in diabetic mice. In human aortic endothelial cells exposed to high glucose/tumor necrosis factor–α or serum from patients with coronary artery disease, EZH2 blockade via GSK-126 or short hairpin RNA suppressed EndMT and reversed transcriptional programs assessed by RNA sequencing, including COL4A1 and NR2F2. These findings identify EZH2 as a driver of EndMT in diabetes-associated atherosclerosis and highlight EZH2 inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy to limit vascular pathology.
Inhibition of an enzyme EZH2 preserves endothelial cell identity and protects vessels from plaque development in diabetes.

sec.p: Received 2025 Dec 7; Accepted 2026 Apr 22; Collection date 2026 May 29.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality among individuals with diabetes, with atherosclerosis being a major underlying pathology (1). Diabetes accelerates atherosclerotic plaque development through multiple mechanisms, including chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and endothelial dysfunction (2). Among these, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), a process whereby endothelial cells lose their characteristic markers and acquire mesenchymal features, has emerged as a critical contributor to vascular remodeling and plaque progression in atherosclerosis (3, 4). Despite substantial advances in cardiometabolic care, including widespread use of statins, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and emerging multihormone incretin therapies, residual cardiovascular risk in diabetes remains appreciable, with many patients experiencing recurrent cardiovascular events. This gap persists across a spectrum of cardio-kidney-metabolic (CKM) phenotypes, especially in individuals with long-standing hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, and chronic low-grade inflammation. These observations underscore the need for complementary, mechanism-based interventions that address nonclassical drivers of vascular risk, including epigenetic programming within the atheroma microenvironment.

A recent study has highlighted the importance of epigenetic regulation in the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis (5). Epigenetic modifications, such as histone methylation, modulate gene expression without altering the DNA sequence, thereby influencing cellular phenotype and function. Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), a histone methyltransferase and the catalytic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), mediates trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine-27 (H3K27me3), a repressive chromatin mark (6). EZH2 has been implicated in various pathological processes, including cancer, fibrosis, and, more recently, vascular disease including atherosclerosis (7–10). However, its specific role in mediating EndMT in the context of diabetes-associated atherosclerosis remains poorly understood.

Given the growing recognition of EndMT as a driver of vascular pathology and the emerging role of EZH2 in vascular disease, we hypothesized that EZH2 may contribute to EndMT and thereby promote atherosclerosis in diabetes. Chromatin remodeling is reversible, and emerging evidence supports the clinical application of chromatin-modifying agents for the prevention and treatment of CVD (11). In this study, we investigated the functional role of EZH2 in human atherosclerotic plaques and in a diabetic Apoe−/− mouse model. We further explored the therapeutic potential of pharmacological EZH2 inhibition using GSK-126, which is more than 1000-fold selective for EZH2 over other methyltransferases (12), in both in vivo and in vitro models of EndMT. Our findings provide insights into the epigenetic mechanisms underlying diabetes-associated atherosclerosis and suggest that targeting EZH2 may represent a promising vasculoprotective strategy.

sec.title: EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 levels are increased in diabetes
sec.p: We first evaluated the abundance of EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 in human carotid endarterectomy specimens from individuals with and without diabetes. Immunohistochemical staining using an anti-H3K27me3 antibody revealed a more than twofold increase in H3K27me3 levels in specimens from diabetic subjects compared with those from individuals without diabetes (Fig. 1, A and B). To further investigate this epigenetic modification, we assessed H3K27me3 levels specifically in aortic endothelial cells from diabetic and nondiabetic Apoe−/− mice. Diabetes was induced in Apoe−/− mice via streptozotocin (STZ) administration, followed by a 10-week observation period before immunofluorescence analysis of aortic tissue using antibodies against CD31 and H3K27me3 (Fig. 1C). As expected, STZ-treated diabetic mice exhibited significantly elevated blood glucose and HbA1c levels compared with nondiabetic controls (Fig. 1, D and E). CD31 staining delineated the aortic endothelial layer, within which H3K27me3 levels were markedly increased in diabetic mice relative to nondiabetic counterparts (Fig. 1, F and G).

sec.title: EZH2 inhibition with GSK-126 attenuates atherosclerosis in diabetes in Apoe−/− mice
sec.p: We next evaluated the therapeutic potential of EZH2 inhibition in diabetes-associated atherosclerosis by conducting a 10-week intervention study using GSK-126 in diabetic Apoe−/− mice (Fig. 2A). Diabetic Apoe−/− mice exhibited significantly reduced body weight gain and elevated blood glucose and HbA1c levels compared to nondiabetic controls (Fig. 2, B to D). To confirm effective EZH2 inhibition by GSK-126, we assessed EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 activity in cardiac tissue using a commercially available assay. As GSK-126 was administered systemically, cardiac tissue served as a proxy for EZH2 activity, whereas aortic tissue was reserved for downstream analyses. Diabetic mice showed increased H3K27me3 activity relative to controls, which was significantly reduced by GSK-126 treatment (fig. S1). GSK-126 treatment did not alter blood glucose, body weight, or HbA1c levels in either diabetic or nondiabetic mice (Fig. 2, B to D). HbA1c levels remained unchanged before and after GSK-126 administration in diabetic mice (Fig. 2E). In addition, lipid profiles, including total cholesterol, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein (HDL), low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and LDL-to-HDL ratio, were unaffected by GSK-126 (Table 1), indicating that its effects are independent of glycemic and lipid control. As expected, diabetic Apoe−/− mice developed significantly larger atherosclerotic plaques, with increased lesion areas observed throughout the aortic arch, thoracic, and abdominal regions (Fig. 2, F to J). Although GSK-126 had no effect in nondiabetic Apoe−/− mice, it significantly reduced atherosclerotic burden in diabetic mice (Fig. 2, F to J). Histological analysis of the aortic root via hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining confirmed increased lesion size in diabetic mice, which was markedly reduced following GSK-126 treatment (Fig. 3, A and B).

sec.p: To assess the role of EZH2 in endothelial cells, particularly within the context of EndMT, we performed immunofluorescence staining of aortic sinus sections. We used antibodies CD31, an established endothelial cell marker, and fibroblast activation protein (FAP), a fibroblast-specific marker known to be expressed in atherosclerotic plaques but not in endothelial cells (13–15). The coexpression of FAP and CD31 (FAP+CD31+) served as an indicator of EndMT (Fig. 3, C and D). Aortic sinuses from diabetic mice showed a significant increase in FAP+CD31+ endothelial cells, indicating diabetes-induced EndMT (Fig. 3, C and D). Notably, GSK-126 treatment significantly reduced the proportion of FAP+CD31+ cells in diabetic mice compared to vehicle-treated controls (Fig. 3, C and D), thereby further supporting its protective role against diabetes-associated vascular remodeling and EndMT.

sec.title: Role of EZH2 in EndMT under high glucose conditions
sec.p: To further elucidate the role of EZH2 in EndMT under high glucose (HG) conditions, we used an in vitro model using human aortic endothelial cells (HAECs), short hairpin RNA (shRNA)–mediated EZH2 knockdown, and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq). Initially, we tested whether pharmacological inhibition of EZH2 with GSK-126 could suppress EndMT in vitro using a well-established model (16). HAECs were stimulated with tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α) (5 ng/ml) under HG conditions (25 mM), with or without GSK-126 (5 μM) for 72 hours (Fig. 4A). Morphological assessments including the quantitative analysis of cell shape metrics revealed that HAECs exposed to TNF-α and HG adopted a spindle-shaped, fibroblast-like morphology characteristic of EndMT with the number of cells with EndMT cell shape metrics is increased under EndMT conditions (fig. S2). This phenotypic transition was prevented by GSK-126 treatment, indicating a protective effect against EndMT (fig. S2). EZH2 activity, as measured by H3K27me3 levels, was elevated in HAECs exposed to TNF-α and HG but was significantly suppressed by GSK-126 despite the presence of EndMT-inducing stimuli (Fig. 4B). Consistent with the in vivo findings, immunofluorescence staining showed an ~3-fold increase in the expression of the EndMT marker FAP in HAECs stimulated with TNF-α under HG conditions compared to unstimulated cells in normal glucose (Fig. 4, C and D). Notably, GSK-126 treatment significantly reduced FAP expression in these cells, confirming its inhibitory effect on EndMT (Fig. 4, C and D). Similarly, immunofluorescence staining for α–smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and fibronectin, well-known mesenchymal markers, showed increased expression under EndMT conditions, which was markedly reduced by GSK-126 treatment (fig. S3, A to E). Real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis further validated these findings, showing up-regulation of α-SMA gene expression in HAECs exposed to TNF-α and HG. This increase was significantly blunted by GSK-126 treatment (fig. S3C), reinforcing the role of EZH2 in mediating EndMT under HG conditions.

sec.title: EZH2 knockdown attenuates FAP expression under EndMT conditions
sec.p: EZH2 was successfully knocked down in HAECs using lentiviral transduction (Fig. 4E). Gene expression analysis via RT-PCR confirmed a marked reduction in EZH2 mRNA levels compared to nontarget controls (Fig. 4F). Correspondingly, immunofluorescence staining revealed decreased H3K27me3 levels in EZH2-deficient HAECs (Fig. 4G), indicating effective epigenetic modulation. To assess the impact of EZH2 knockdown on EndMT, both EZH2-deficient and control HAECs were exposed to TNF-α and HG for 72 hours. Immunostaining showed elevated expression of the mesenchymal marker FAP in nontarget HAECs under EndMT conditions (Fig. 4, H and I). Notably, FAP expression was significantly reduced in EZH2 knockdown cells, validating that EZH2 contributes to EndMT (Fig. 4, H and I).

sec.title: EZH2 gene targets in EndMT under HG conditions
sec.p: Having established that EZH2 inhibition—either genetically via shRNA or pharmacologically using GSK-126—blocks EndMT in HAECs, we next sought to identify EZH2-regulated gene targets in EndMT under HG conditions. RNA-seq of HAECs exposed to EndMT-inducing stimuli (TNF-α and HG), with or without GSK-126 treatment, revealed 76 genes whose expression was restored upon EZH2 inhibition (Fig. 5, A and B, and table S3). Notably, these EZH2-regulated genes included several key players in EndMT, such as COL4A1, COL12A1, TGFβ2, SERPINE2, MMRN1, NOS3, NOTCH4, CD34, NR2F2, POSTN, and PIEZO2 (Fig. 5, B and C). Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis using Partek Flow identified pathways affected by EZH2 inhibition, including blood vessel morphogenesis, collagen trimer formation, regulation of blood pressure, cell adhesion, extracellular matrix (ECM) organization, signal transduction, and response to stimuli (Fig. 5C). The alluvial plot highlighted the distribution of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across the top 10 enriched pathways, with genes such as COL4A1 and TGFβ2 appearing in multiple pathways (Fig. 5C). To validate these findings, we examined the effect of EZH2 inhibition using GSK-126 on selected EndMT-associated DEGs. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis confirmed that GSK-126 mitigated the TNF-α– and HG-induced up-regulation of COL4A1 and NEDD9 (Fig. 5, D to F) and reversed the down-regulation of MMRN1 and NR2F2 (Fig. 5, G and H), consistent with the RNA-seq results (Fig. 5B and table S3). To assess whether EZH2 inhibition and the associated reduction in H3K27me3 influenced cellular senescence, we interrogated our RNA-seq dataset for senescence-associated signatures, including the SenMayo panel. No significant increase in expression of these genes was observed following GSK-126 inhibition. Of the hundreds of genes included in SenMayo, expression of only two, SERPINE2 and ANGPTL4, was reduced following EZH2 inhibition (table S3). Both genes are known to be expressed by mesenchymal cells including vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) and are typically up-regulated in EndMT and atherosclerosis rather than being specific markers of senescence (17–19). These findings indicate that EZH2 inhibition does not induce a broad senescence-associated transcriptional program.

sec.title: GSK-126 prevents EndMT induced by patient-derived serum in HAECs
sec.p: To assess the translational relevance of our findings, we developed an ex vivo disease model by exposing HAECs to serum from patients with CVD and with and without diabetes, recruited through the Alfred Hospital. All participants had angiographically confirmed atherosclerotic CVD (ASCVD). Clinical characteristics, including age, body mass index (BMI), blood pressure, and lipid profiles, were comparable between diabetic and nondiabetic groups (Table 2). Medications included standard cardiovascular therapies [angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, aspirin, and statins], with patients with diabetes additionally receiving antidiabetic agents such as SGLT2 inhibitors, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, and metformin. HAECs were cultured in serum-containing media for 72 hours, with or without the EZH2 inhibitor GSK-126 (Fig. 6A). EndMT was assessed by immunofluorescence staining for FAP. Compared to cells maintained in standard culture media, HAECs exposed to serum from patients with and without diabetes showed increased FAP expression, indicating induction of EndMT (Fig. 6, B and C). Notably, FAP expression was significantly higher in cells treated with diabetic serum in combination with added glucose, suggesting a more pronounced EndMT response (Fig. 6, B and C). Treatment with GSK-126 markedly reduced FAP expression in HAECs exposed to both diabetic and nondiabetic serum, demonstrating that EZH2 inhibition effectively blocks serum-induced EndMT (Fig. 6, B and C).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study provides compelling evidence that the epigenetic regulator EZH2 plays a pivotal role in promoting EndMT in the context of diabetes-associated atherosclerosis. By integrating in vivo, in vitro, and human ex vivo models, we demonstrate that EZH2 activity is elevated under diabetic conditions and contributes to EndMT (Fig. 7), a process increasingly recognized as a key contributor to atherosclerotic plaque progression and instability (20). Notably, pharmacological inhibition of EZH2 using GSK-126 notably attenuated EndMT and reduced associated atherosclerotic burden, as shown by Sudan IV and H&E staining, emphasizing EZH2 as a promising therapeutic target in diabetic vascular disease.

caption.title: EZH2 promotes EndMT in diabetes-associated atherosclerosis, which is attenuated by GSK-126.
caption.p: EZH2 activity is increased under diabetic conditions, promoting EndMT and contributing to atherosclerotic plaque progression. Across in vivo, in vitro, and human ex vivo models, elevated EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 was associated with enhanced EndMT. Pharmacological inhibition with GSK-126 reduced EndMT and decreased atherosclerotic burden, highlighting EZH2 as a potential therapeutic target. Created in BioRender. Jandeleit-Dahm, K. (2026) https://BioRender.com/sw9j00o.

sec.p: EZH2, the catalytic subunit of PRC2, mediates transcriptional repression via H3K27me3. We first observed a marked increase in H3K27me3 levels in carotid plaques from patients with diabetes, suggesting that hyperglycemia enhances EZH2 activity. A previous study has reported endothelial-specific enrichment of H3K27me3 in human plaques, supporting the notion that localized epigenetic modifications contribute to atherosclerosis (7, 21, 22). Although direct endothelial-specific detection of H3K27me3 in human plaque specimens used in our study was not feasible, we addressed this limitation using a diabetic Apoe−/− mouse model. Here, we confirmed elevated EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 levels specifically in the aortic endothelium, reinforcing the relevance of our findings to endothelial pathophysiology.

To assess therapeutic potential, we conducted a preclinical intervention study using GSK-126, a specific EZH2 inhibitor (23). GSK-126 exerted atheroprotective effects independent of metabolic parameters as this drug did not alter glucose levels or other systemic indices such as lipid levels. This suggests a direct vascular mechanism with GSK-126 treatment substantially reducing diabetes-induced EndMT, as evidenced by decreased FAP expression in the aortic endothelium, indicating a protective role of this drug against diabetes-associated vascular remodeling.

In vitro, HAECs exposed to TNF-α and HG exhibited hallmark EndMT features, including spindle-shaped morphology and up-regulation of mesenchymal markers such as FAP and α-SMA (24). Both pharmacological inhibition and genetic knockdown of EZH2 suppressed these changes, confirming that EZH2 activity is essential for EndMT under diabetic conditions. GSK-126 not only reduced H3K27me3 levels but also reversed mesenchymal marker expression, even in the continued presence of EndMT-inducing stimuli such as glucose and TNF-α, highlighting the potential of EZH2 inhibition to restore endothelial identity.

RNA-seq further elucidated the molecular mechanisms underlying EZH2-mediated EndMT under HG conditions. EZH2 inhibition restored the expression of 76 genes, including key regulators of endothelial and mesenchymal identity such as COL4A1, COL12A1, TGFβ2, SERPINE2, MMRN1, NOS3, NOTCH4, CD34, POSTN, and PIEZO2. GO analysis revealed enrichment in pathways related to vascular development, ECM organization, and signal transduction. qPCR validation confirmed that GSK-126 mitigated the up-regulation of fibrotic genes (e.g., COL4A1 and NEDD9) and rescued endothelial-associated genes (e.g., MMRN1 and NR2F2), consistent with previously reported transcriptomic findings (25, 26).

Our results align with and extend prior studies. For instance, Chen et al. demonstrated that EndMT promotes atherosclerosis progression, whereas Evrard et al. provided lineage-tracing evidence that EndMT-derived fibroblast-like cells are prevalent in plaques (3, 20). Single-cell RNA-seq of endothelial-enriched cells from the diabetic mouse heart and aorta identified distinct clusters expressing mesenchymal markers, further supporting the concept of endothelial plasticity during diabetic atherogenesis. These findings collectively underscore the pathological relevance of EndMT and the need for targeted interventions (27).

Given the limited therapeutic options that specifically address endothelial plasticity and its contribution to plaque instability, epigenetic modulation offers a promising and potentially disease-modifying approach. The ability of GSK-126 to attenuate mesenchymal features both in vivo and ex vivo highlights its potential as an epigenetic therapy for diabetic atherosclerosis. EZH2’s role in promoting EndMT may have broader implications as EndMT contributes not only to lesion initiation but also to fibrous cap thinning and plaque vulnerability. Cells undergoing EndMT can enhance ECM production, inflammation, and smooth muscle–like phenotypes within plaques. Thus, targeting EZH2’s methyltransferase activity may confer dual benefits: limiting plaque growth and enhancing stability.

The therapeutic promise of EZH2 inhibition is further supported by the reversibility of epigenetic modifications and the favorable safety profile of GSK-126 in clinical trials for other indications (28). In our study, GSK-126 treatment of nondiabetic control mice or in HAECs under normal serum and glucose conditions showed no effects on endothelial morphology. Our findings suggest that EZH2 inhibition could serve as a vasculoprotective strategy to mitigate EndMT-driven plaque progression in diabetes, potentially addressing residual cardiovascular risk not addressed by conventional therapies.

To assess translational relevance, we developed a human ex vivo model using serum from patients with CVD and with and without diabetes. HAECs exposed to patient serum exhibited increased FAP expression, indicative of serum-induced EndMT. Notably, serum from patients with diabetes elicited a more robust EndMT response. GSK-126 treatment significantly reduced FAP expression in HAECs exposed to both diabetic and nondiabetic serum, demonstrating that EZH2 inhibition can counteract circulating pro-EndMT factors in human disease.

Our findings align with the concept of glycemic memory, wherein prior hyperglycemia imprints durable epigenetic changes that sustain vascular risk even after metabolic improvement. Repressive chromatin remodeling via EZH2-mediated H3K27me3 provides a plausible mechanism for such memory within vascular and immune cell compartments. By attenuating H3K27me3, EZH2 inhibition may partially reverse pro-atherogenic transcriptional programs that underpin the legacy effect (29), complementing contemporary therapies that optimize hemodynamic and metabolic parameters.

Although the main emphasizes of Apoe-STZ model is on hyperglycemia and dyslipidemia, EZH2 activity has been implicated in inflammatory pathways, adipogenesis and obesity (30, 31). We anticipate that the EZH2-dependent regulatory signature contributes to vascular dysfunction in diet-induced obesity and various CKM states with testing in high-fat diet models and leptin-pathway mutants potentially important to establish generalizability. Future studies should integrate metabolic phenotyping (insulin sensitivity, and adipokines), tissue-specific EZH2 perturbation (endothelium, macrophages, and smooth muscle), and atherosclerosis readouts to delineate context-dependent effects.

Together, these findings establish EZH2 as a central epigenetic regulator of EndMT in diabetes-associated atherosclerosis. The identification of EZH2-regulated gene networks provides mechanistic insight into how epigenetic reprogramming contributes to vascular pathology. Although our study highlights the therapeutic potential of EZH2 inhibition, several limitations warrant further investigation. These include the long-term safety studies to evaluate tissue-specific effects. Female mice are resistant to STZ and exhibit lower susceptibility to atherosclerosis, and therefore only male mice were used in this study. Given that sex differences influence both atherosclerosis progression and epigenetic regulation, our findings may not be generalizable to females. Future studies incorporating both sexes are needed to more comprehensively define the therapeutic potential of EZH2 inhibition. Although our serum-based ex vivo model demonstrates that diabetic conditions exacerbate EndMT and that GSK-126 exerts vasculoprotective effects, further preclinical and clinical studies are needed to evaluate the durability, safety, and translational potential of EZH2 inhibition. Also, all patients with diabetes included in the ex vivo experiments were receiving glucose-lowering therapy and had well-controlled glycemia. As a result, the study population may not represent individuals with poorly controlled or uncontrolled diabetes, in whom hyperglycemia-driven epigenetic dysregulations are typically more pronounced. This limits the generalizability of the findings to the broader diabetic population. In addition, exploring combination therapies that pair EZH2 inhibitors with other agents may enhance therapeutic efficacy and provide a more comprehensive strategy to mitigate vascular complications in diabetes. Human atherosclerotic tissue studies are inherently constrained by sample availability and clinical heterogeneity. Despite careful matching for age and sex, we acknowledge the limited sample size, which may reduce the power to detect subtle effects and increase susceptibility to residual confounding. Nevertheless, the concordance of findings across human specimens, ex vivo assays, and mouse models enhances the robustness of the key findings. Prospective studies with larger cohorts and longitudinal sampling will further define the translational relevance of these findings. In addition, although our data strongly support a central role for EZH2 activity in EndMT in the context of atherosclerosis in diabetes, we acknowledge that EZH2 inhibition may also influence other vascular cell populations. GSK-126 has previously been shown to exert anti-inflammatory effects in several disease models, including mechanisms involved in monocyte-driven inflammatory pathways. Furthermore, GSK-126 has been reported to reduce atherosclerosis even in nondiabetic high-fat diet models, suggesting that EZH2 inhibition may exert multicellular vascular effects beyond the endothelium. Although our work primarily focused on EndMT, we cannot exclude additional contributions from macrophages, vascular smooth muscle cells, or other immune cell populations. Future studies using cell type–specific EZH2 deletion models as well as cell-specific multiomics analyses will be essential to definitively delineate the cell-specific effects of EZH2 inhibition.
Nonetheless, our data support the continued development of epigenetic-based strategies to restore endothelial function and reduce atherosclerotic burden in high-risk diabetic populations.

sec.title: Ethics statements
sec.p: All preclinical experimental procedures were conducted in accordance with the ARRIVE guidelines and adhered to the standards set by the Australian National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). Ethical approval for animal studies was obtained from the Alfred Medical Research and Education Precinct (AMREP) Animal Services Ethics Committee (project no. P1995). For studies involving human plasma and carotid endarterectomy specimens, ethical approval was granted by the Alfred Human Research Ethics Committee (approval nos. 232/17 and 24/07). Participants were recruited from the Alfred Hospital (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia) and provided written informed consent for the use of their specimens in research.

sec.title: Immunohistochemical staining of human carotid artery specimens
sec.p: Human carotid artery specimens were collected during carotid endarterectomy procedures. Tissues were fixed in 4% formalin, decalcified using 10% nitric acid (v/v), and embedded in paraffin before sectioning. Immunohistochemical analysis was performed to assess H3K27me3 levels in carotid plaques from patients with and without diabetes as previously described (32). These paraffin-embedded sections are cut onto slides, deparaffinized in xylene, and rehydrated through graded alcohols. To unmask the H3K27me3 epitope, the slides undergo heat-mediated antigen retrieval. After cooling, endogenous peroxidase activity and nonspecific binding sites are blocked using appropriate blocking solutions. The tissue sections are then incubated with the primary anti-H3K27me3 antibody (1:300; Abcam 07-449) for overnight. Following this, a species-specific secondary antibody is applied. Last, the slides are counterstained with hematoxylin to provide nuclear contrast and examined microscopically for qualitative or quantitative assessment of H3K27me3 levels.

sec.title: Mice and preclinical intervention studies
sec.p: Male Apoe−/− mice on a C57BL/6 background were used to model diabetes-associated atherosclerosis. We initially performed a pilot study to identify endothelial selective H3K27me3 levels. At 6 weeks of age, mice were randomly assigned to either nondiabetic control or diabetic groups. Diabetes was induced via intraperitoneal injection of STZ (55 mg/kg body weight) for 5 consecutive days. Control mice received citrate buffer as a vehicle. Mice were fed a standard chow diet (SF00-100; Specialty Feeds, Glen Forrest, WA, Australia). Mice were monitored for 10 weeks following diabetes induction. For the intervention study, 5 weeks post–STZ administration, both diabetic and nondiabetic control mice received daily intraperitoneal injections of either vehicle (Captisol) or the EZH2 inhibitor GSK-126 (50 mg/kg body weight) for an additional 5 weeks (n = 6 to 11 per group). Body weight and blood glucose levels were recorded weekly throughout the study. At study endpoint, mice were euthanized using CO2 inhalation, and tissues were isolated for further analysis. Body weight, tissue weights, HbA1c, and blood glucose levels were measured. Heparinized blood was collected and centrifuged to isolate plasma for lipid profiling, which was performed using standard enzymatic assays with commercial kits, as previously described (33). Tissues were harvested for histological and molecular analyses.

sec.title: Histology
sec.p: Aortae were excised and cleaned in normal saline to remove perivascular adipose tissue. Atherosclerotic lesion burden was assessed using en face analysis following Sudan IV staining, with quantification of lesions in a blinded manner in the aortic arch, thoracic, and abdominal regions, as previously described (32). For cross-sectional analysis, hearts were embedded in optimal cutting temperature (OCT) compound, frozen, and sectioned through the aortic root. Sections were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and stained with H&E. Images were acquired using a Nikon CI bright-field microscope, and lesion area was quantified using the ImageJ software, calculating the relative lesion area to the total aortic sinus area. Quantitative data from the spatially separated sections were averaged to yield a single value per animal.

sec.title: Study participants and clinical characteristics
sec.p: This study included 16 participants recruited from the Alfred Hospital: 8 with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and 8 without diabetes. All participants had angiographically confirmed ASCVD. Detailed demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 2. Standard cardiovascular therapy comprised angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), ACE inhibitors, acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin), and HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A) reductase inhibitors (statins). Participants with T2DM received guideline-directed antidiabetic treatment, including metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, and DPP-4 inhibitors. Serum samples were isolated and stored at −80°C until use in tissue culture experiments.

sec.title: Cell culture, EndMT induction, and shRNA-mediated EZH2 knockdown
sec.p: Primary HAECs (CC-2535, Lonza, Mount Waverley, Australia) were cultured in EGM-2 medium supplemented with the Endothelial Cell Growth Medium-2 BulletKit (CC-3156 and CC-4176, Lonza) at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2. To induce EndMT, HAECs were stimulated with TNF-α (5 ng/ml) and HG (25 mM) ± GSK-126 (5 μM) for 72 hours. Morphological changes were monitored using a Thermo Fisher Scientific EVOS microscope. For serum-based EndMT induction, HAECs were cultured in EGM-2 medium supplemented with 10% serum from patients with or without diabetes for 72 hours, in the presence or absence of the EZH2 inhibitor GSK-126. As all patients with diabetes were under glucose-lowering therapy with well-controlled glycemia, glucose was supplemented to a final concentration of 25 mM in cultures treated with diabetic serum to mimic hyperglycemic conditions.

EZH2 knockdown was performed using MISSION shRNA-expressing lentiviral vectors (Sigma-Aldrich) targeting human EZH2 (RefSeq: NM_004456). The target sequence used was 5′-TATGATGGTTAACGGTGATCA-3′. Transduction efficiency and knockdown validation were confirmed by qRT-PCR for EZH2 using primers listed in table S2. Cells transduced with MISSION nontargeting shRNA lentiviral vectors were used as controls. Following confirmation of EZH2 knockdown, HAECs were subjected to EndMT-inducing conditions as described above.

sec.title: Immunofluorescence staining
sec.p: Immunofluorescence staining was conducted on tissue sections collected at the conclusion of the in vivo experiments, as well as on HAECs subjected to EndMT-inducing conditions. Tissue sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies targeting H3K27me3 (Abcam, 07-449; 1:200), CD31 (Abcam, ab195277; 1:50), and FAP (Abcam, ab218164; 1:50) to assess their expression in the aortic sinus and aorta (table S1). HAECs were similarly stained overnight at 4°C with antibodies against α-SMA (Abcam, ab21027; 1:300), H3K27me3 (07-449; 1:300), CD31 (ab195277; 1:50), FAP (ab218164; 1:50), and fibronectin (A0245; 1:3000) (table S1). Following primary antibody incubation, both tissue sections and cells were washed and incubated with species-specific fluorescent secondary antibodies (anti-rat, anti-rabbit, or anti-goat) for 1 hour at room temperature. Nuclei were counterstained using Hoechst 33342 (PureBlu, Bio-Rad, 1351304EDU). Fluorescence imaging was performed using a Nikon fluorescence microscope for tissue sections and a Thermo Fisher Scientific EVOS fluorescence microscope for HAECs. Image analysis was carried out using the ImageJ software. Quantification was performed in a blinded manner, with fluorescence intensity normalized to cell number for each image. Five to six images were evaluated from each of three spatially separated aortic root sections per mouse. Data were averaged per mouse and then used for statistical analyses.

sec.title: H3K27me3 activity assay
sec.p: Nuclear protein was extracted using an acid extraction protocol as previously described (34). Protein concentration was quantified, and equal amounts of histone protein were used to assess H3K27me3 methyltransferase activity using the EpiQuik H3K27 Methyltransferase Activity Kit (EpigenTek, P-3042-96) (10). H3K27 methyltransferase activity was calculated using the following formula
All measurements were performed in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.

sec.title: RNA-seq and bioinformatic analysis
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from HAECs exposed to EndMT-inducing conditions and GSK-126 (5 μM) using TRIzol Reagent (Invitrogen, Australia) and the Direct-zol RNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research, USA), following the manufacturer’s protocols as previously described (34). To enrich for mRNA, 1 μg of total RNA was processed using the NEBNext rRNA Depletion Kit (New England Biolabs, USA). Barcoded libraries were prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs), and deep sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq PE 75 platform at the Novogen Company Limited (Hong Kong). Raw sequence reads were trimmed using Skewer (35) and aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38/hg38) using the STAR aligner (36). Gene-level quantification was performed using FeatureCounts with Ensembl transcript annotations (release 103). Downstream analysis was conducted in the Partek Flow software, including normalization and differential gene expression (DGE) analysis using the gene-specific analysis (GSA) methods. Genes with a false discovery rate (FDR) of <0.05 and a fold change of >±2 were considered statistically significant. Heatmaps were generated within Partek Flow to visualize the expression pattern. Functional enrichment and pathway analysis were performed using Partek Flow’s integrated tools. To further explore the relationship between gene expression and biological pathways, DGE and pathway enrichment results were exported to R (v4.2.0) and visualized using the ggplot2 and ggalluvial packages (37, 38). A clustered bubble plot was constructed to illustrate gene expression changes across experimental contrasts, where the bubble size represented statistical significance (FDR), and the color indicated the direction and magnitude of fold change. In parallel, an alluvial plot was used to map genes to enriched pathways. These visualizations were combined to provide an integrated view of gene-level differential expression and associated functional pathways.

sec.title: RT-PCR analysis
sec.p: Quantitative RT-PCR was performed to assess gene expression using primers listed in table S2. cDNA was amplified using the FastStart Universal SYBR Green Master Mix (Roche, Melbourne, Australia) or TaqMan system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on an ABI 7900HT PCR cycler (Applied Biosystems). Relative transcript levels were calculated using the ΔCT method, with normalization to the housekeeping gene H3F3.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All data are presented as means ± SEM. Statistical analyses were conducted using the GraphPad Prism. For comparisons between two groups, the Mann-Whitney U test was used for nonparametric data. For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey’s post hoc test was applied to parametric data, whereas the Kruskal-Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple comparisons was used for nonparametric data. A P value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: All data and code needed to evaluate and reproduce the results in the paper are present in the paper and/or the Supplementary Materials. There are no new materials generated in the study. RNA-seq datasets are deposited in the international public repository Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number GSE316326. GSK-126 was generously provided by the GlaxoSmithKline LLC, USA (GSK) after completing the material transfer agreement between Monash University and GSK. The GSK-126 is a commercially available drug.
